$comment: Every background task in the backend, and how it dies (ADR-CORE-037, ADR-APP-032).
Spawning work creates an entry point: something starts running with nobody above it to report to.
A task that ends quietly — a loop that exits on the first Err, a worker that returns on a closed
channel without a word — is a silent death, and the user's first hint is a feature that stopped
working with nothing in the log.
The crash gate (scripts/lib/crash-gate.mjs, run by `npm run lint`) counts the spawns in every Rust
source file and rejects any it does not find here. Adding a task therefore forces one question to
be answered in writing: HOW DOES THIS ONE DIE? Answer it in `why`.
This file is PROJECT-OWNED: never pinned, never delivered by `governance:update`. A fork inherits
the entries below with the template and maintains its own from there.

src-tauri/src/lib.rs.why: The log bridge (setup): forwards tracing records to the UI log view. On RecvError::Lagged it warns and KEEPS BRIDGING — the receiver is still valid, so the old `while let Ok(..)` loop, which ended the task and silently froze the log view for the rest of the session, is exactly what this entry exists to prevent. On RecvError::Closed the sender is gone (logging is shutting down): it logs that and ends, which is the only way this task is allowed to stop.

src-tauri/src/terminal/mod.rs.why: Two threads per terminal session, and each one has exactly one way to end. (1) The READER blocks on the PTY and ends on EOF — the child exited, which is the normal end — or on a read error, which it logs at debug because on close the fd is torn out from under it deliberately. Before returning it waits for the child and forwards the exit code, so the pump always learns the session is over; if the pump is already gone it logs that and returns, since there is nothing left to read for. (2) The PUMP batches output and is the LAST thread of a session to die, which is why it is the one that announces the exit: it flushes the final bytes, logs the session's exit code and byte count, emits terminal://exit and drops the session from the registry. It ends when the reader reports the end, or when the mpsc disconnects. Neither thread can end silently: every exit path above logs, and the user-visible one (the exit event) is emitted after the last flush, never before it.

src-tauri/src/terminal/environment.rs.why: One short-lived thread, once per process, that asks a login shell what environment it would set. It ends when the shell exits — normally in milliseconds. If it takes longer than CAPTURE_TIMEOUT the CALLER stops waiting and continues with a short PATH; the thread itself is deliberately left to finish into a dropped channel rather than killed, because it is blocked on a child process that cannot be torn down safely from here. It cannot end silently: the success path logs the captured variable count and PATH at info, every failure path (non-zero status, spawn error, timeout) logs a warning naming what was lost, and the consequence — commands the user has installed appearing 'not found' — is visible in their own terminal.

src-tauri/src/git/fetch.rs.why: The fetch itself. `Command` has no timeout, so the child runs on a thread the caller waits on with a deadline (20s). HOW IT DIES: it sends the process result down a channel and returns. If the deadline passes first the caller has already moved on and the receiver is gone — the send fails, the result is discarded, and the thread ends. That is deliberate: the child cannot be killed safely from here, so the thread is allowed to finish into nothing rather than be abandoned mid-write. Nothing is lost, because the caller has already reported the timeout to the user (ADR-PROJ-002).

src-tauri/src/commands/mod.rs.why: Command work moved off Tauri's MAIN thread with `spawn_blocking`, because a synchronous command blocks window events and IPC for as long as its child process runs — measured: `agent_usage` shells out to `claude -p /usage` at ~1.5 s and made the Agent tool take that long to paint. **None of these tasks can die silently, and the shape is the same for every one of them:** the closure does the work and returns a value; the command `await`s the JoinHandle and maps a join error into an `AppError` that carries the command's name. That error travels back over IPC, where `Serialize for AppError` logs it at error level (mem:logging-contract) and the UI shows it in the panel that asked. A panicked closure therefore surfaces as a failed call with a message, never as a panel that stays empty — `container_stats` is the one deliberate exception: it degrades to an empty list after logging at error, because 'no containers' is the answer it already gives when Docker is absent, and an error banner there would be worse than the truth it can still show. Here: `container_stats` (~2 s `docker stats`), `install_direnv` (a package manager — minutes), `environment_status` and `set_project_environment` (both spawn `direnv`), and `open_path`, which hands a file to the platform's default application — the one deliberate exception to "the frontend must not choose what runs", overruled by the maintainer with the reasoning recorded at the command. And `import_terminal_theme`, which opens the NATIVE file picker: the plugin's `blocking_pick_file` must not run on the main thread, so it runs here — it ends when the user chooses or closes the dialog, and a closed dialog returns `Ok(None)`, which the UI draws as nothing happening rather than as a failure. A panic inside it takes the same route as every other closure above: a join error carrying the command's name, logged once at the IPC boundary and shown where the press was."

src-tauri/src/commands/terminal.rs.why: Command work moved off Tauri's MAIN thread with `spawn_blocking`, because a synchronous command blocks window events and IPC for as long as its child process runs — measured: `agent_usage` shells out to `claude -p /usage` at ~1.5 s and made the Agent tool take that long to paint. **None of these tasks can die silently, and the shape is the same for every one of them:** the closure does the work and returns a value; the command `await`s the JoinHandle and maps a join error into an `AppError` that carries the command's name. That error travels back over IPC, where `Serialize for AppError` logs it at error level (mem:logging-contract) and the UI shows it in the panel that asked. A panicked closure therefore surfaces as a failed call with a message, never as a panel that stays empty — `container_stats` is the one deliberate exception: it degrades to an empty list after logging at error, because 'no containers' is the answer it already gives when Docker is absent, and an error banner there would be worse than the truth it can still show. Here: `agent_usage`, the one this was found on; `tmux_sessions`, which starts `tmux list-sessions` for the attach picker; and `tmux_kill_session` / `tmux_rename_session`, which start `tmux kill-session` / `rename-session` for the tmux tool. The last two are the only DESTRUCTIVE work in this app, so their failure mode matters more than most: the closure returns the `Result` and the command `await`s it, so a tmux that refused — a name that no longer exists, a rename onto one that does — surfaces as a failed call carrying tmux's own stderr, shown in the tool that asked. A panicked closure is a join error with the command's name. Neither can end as a session silently not killed while the row disappears from the list. And `agent_chain`, which starts `tmux list-panes` to find out which processes belong to THIS tab — the only thing that separates two agents working in one repository. It is polled every few seconds, so running it on the main thread would make every keystroke in every terminal wait for a tmux call; a join error surfaces as a failed call named `reading the chain failed`, and the tool shows its error state rather than an empty panel that looks like 'no agent here'.

src-tauri/src/commands/git.rs.why: Command work moved off Tauri's MAIN thread with `spawn_blocking`, because a synchronous command blocks window events and IPC for as long as its child process runs — measured: `agent_usage` shells out to `claude -p /usage` at ~1.5 s and made the Agent tool take that long to paint. **None of these tasks can die silently, and the shape is the same for every one of them:** the closure does the work and returns a value; the command `await`s the JoinHandle and maps a join error into an `AppError` that carries the command's name. That error travels back over IPC, where `Serialize for AppError` logs it at error level (mem:logging-contract) and the UI shows it in the panel that asked. A panicked closure therefore surfaces as a failed call with a message, never as a panel that stays empty — `container_stats` is the one deliberate exception: it degrades to an empty list after logging at error, because 'no containers' is the answer it already gives when Docker is absent, and an error banner there would be worse than the truth it can still show. Here: `git_fetch`, which is bounded by a remote host rather than by us.

src-tauri/src/notes/git.rs.why: Every git call the notes sync makes. `Command` has no timeout, so the child runs on a thread the caller waits on with a deadline (45s — longer than the auto-fetch's, because a first push may be a clone's worth of notes over a slow link). HOW IT DIES: it sends the process result down a channel and returns. If the deadline passes first the caller has already moved on and the receiver is gone; the send fails, the result is dropped, and the thread ends. Deliberate, and the same trade as git/fetch.rs: the child cannot be killed safely from here, so the thread finishes into nothing rather than being abandoned mid-write — and nothing is lost, because the caller has already recorded the timeout as the sync's last error, which the settings panel shows verbatim. A sync that fails is never fatal: the notes are written locally and stay readable either way (ADR-PROJ-004).

src-tauri/src/commands/notes.rs.why: `off_thread`: the one `spawn_blocking` every notes command routes its filesystem and git work through, so none of it runs on Tauri's main thread (it froze the window for the length of a git call — measured at 3.4 s at startup). It dies with the work it was given: the closure returns, the JoinHandle resolves, and the command awaits it. A panic inside cannot vanish, because the JoinError is logged at error and turned into an AppError the caller receives — the command fails visibly instead of the panel silently never filling.
